The company reports around $115 million in annual revenue and approximately 1,600 employees. CureMD markets itself as providing \"the most affordable EHR, RCM & PM for any size of practice\" and claims over 30,000 practices, 109,000 users across 44 states and 32+ medical specialties. They also report supporting 300+ public health departments across 25 states.\n\nCureMD is a mid-size ambulatory EHR vendor competing in the crowded small-to-mid practice segment. They offer an integrated, cloud-based platform combining clinical (EHR), administrative (practice management), financial (revenue cycle management/billing), and patient engagement (patient portal) capabilities. They sell directly and also offer outsourced billing services. The company has received recognition from KLAS and Black Book rankings. CureMD targets ambulatory practices from solo providers to multi-site groups, including specialty practices, urgent care, behavioral health, and rural/public health settings. A January 2026 press release announced a \"Rural Health Accelerator Package\" specifically targeting CMS Rural Health Transformation Program requirements.\n\n## Product: CureMD SMART Cloud\n\nCHPL ID: 11246 (version 10g, certified 2023-03-02)\n\n### What It Is\n\nCureMD SMART Cloud is a comprehensive, cloud-based ambulatory healthcare platform that integrates EHR, practice management, patient portal, and revenue cycle management into a single system. It is certified across 35+ ONC criteria spanning clinical data (a)(1)–(a)(14), care coordination (b)(1)–(b)(3), patient portal (e)(1), public health reporting (f)(1)–(f)(7), and API/FHIR access (g)(7)–(g)(10)). The breadth of certification confirms this is a full-featured ambulatory EHR, not a niche module.\n\nThe certified module appears to be the entire platform — CureMD does not appear to sell separate EHR, PM, or billing modules as independently certified products. The CHPL metadata describes intended users as \"Ambulatory Physicians, Nurses and Administrative Staff Members.\"\n\n### Users & Market\n\n**Target users:** Physicians, nurses, billing staff, practice managers, and patients (via portal). The platform is designed for ambulatory settings including solo practices, group practices, multi-site organizations, FQHCs, urgent care, and rural health clinics.\n\n**Specialties:** CureMD explicitly supports 32+ specialties including: Internal Medicine, Primary Care, Pediatrics, Cardiology, Pulmonary, Dermatology, Gastroenterology, Behavioral Health/Psychiatry, Allergy/Immunology, Endocrinology, Infectious Disease, Nephrology, Neurology, OB/GYN, Oncology, Ophthalmology, Orthopedics, Otolaryngology, Pain Management, Physical Medicine, Podiatry, Rheumatology, Sleep Medicine, Urology, General Surgery, Hand Surgery, Vascular Surgery, Ambulatory Surgery, Speech Therapy, Rehabilitative Medicine, House Call, Urgent Care, and Public Sector.\n\n**Scale:** Claims 30,000+ practices, 109,000+ users, 44 states. Revenue ~$115M, ~1,600 employees.\n\n**Notable deployment:** 300+ public health departments across 25 states (per Jan 2026 press release).\n\n### Modules & Functionality\n\nBased on vendor materials, feature pages, press releases, and third-party reviews, CureMD SMART Cloud includes the following integrated modules and features:\n\n**Electronic Health Records (EHR/EMR):**\n- Clinical charting with customizable, specialty-specific templates (30+ specialties)\n- Patient encounter documentation with flexible charting options\n- Medical history recording\n- Vital signs tracking and trending\n- Problem lists, diagnoses, and assessment/plan documentation\n- Clinical decision support (drug-drug, drug-allergy, drug-diagnosis interaction checking; age/weight-based dose adjustments)\n- AI-powered medical scribe for automated documentation and coding\n- Reusable order sets\n- Clinical summaries and visit notes\n\n**E-Prescribing:**\n- Electronic prescribing via Surescripts integration to 40,000+ pharmacies\n- Controlled substance prescribing (EPCS)\n- Medication reconciliation\n- Prescription benefits, history, formulary, and eligibility checking\n- Drug interaction and adverse reaction alerts\n- Prescription tracking and refill management\n\n**Laboratory Integration:**\n- Electronic lab ordering and results receipt (integrates with LabCorp, Quest Diagnostics, and others)\n- Lab result trending and comparison (current vs. past)\n- Abnormal result alerts and task assignment\n- Imaging/radiology order integration and diagnostic report viewing\n\n**Practice Management (PM):**\n- Patient demographics and registration\n- Appointment scheduling (multi-provider, multi-location)\n- Recurring appointments and administrative alerts\n- Digital check-in\n- Insurance eligibility verification (real-time, pre-visit)\n- Referral management\n- Document management (scans, images, x-rays, faxes)\n- E-fax capability\n- Multi-location management\n- Inventory management with barcode scanning and central supply chain\n- KPI dashboards and business intelligence reporting\n\n**Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) / Billing:**\n- Automatic charge capture\n- Rules-based claims scrubbing (98%+ first-pass acceptance rate claimed)\n- Electronic claim submission\n- Electronic payment posting\n- Denial management with automatic tracking\n- Patient balance collection at check-in/check-out\n- Point-of-sale credit card processing\n- Financial reporting\n- Payer management\n- Outsourced billing services also available as a separate offering\n\n**Patient Portal (LEAP — Life Extension & Advancement Platform):**\n- Patient access to health records and clinical summaries\n- Lab/radiology results viewing with simplified explanations\n- Medication tracking with adherence reminders\n- Secure messaging between patients and care teams\n- Appointment scheduling and management\n- Digital check-in and registration\n- Online payments, co-pay tracking, billing transparency\n- Post-visit summaries and treatment plan access\n- Family/caregiver proxy access\n- Wearable device integration (Apple Watch, Fitbit) for vitals monitoring\n- AI-powered care gap alerts and preventive care recommendations\n- CureDoc conversational AI for 24/7 Q&A and scheduling\n- Health education content\n- Telehealth access\n\n**Telehealth:**\n- Integrated HD video telemedicine platform\n- Pre-visit forms, consent signing, and online payment\n- Remote consultations scheduled alongside in-person visits\n\n**Chronic Care Management (CCM):**\n- Patient identification and eligibility screening\n- Individualized care plan creation (goals, symptoms, problems, medications, allergies)\n- Time tracking for billable activities\n- Engagement tracking and care coordination documentation\n- Consent management and enrollment\n- Medicare CCM/PCM billing (CPT 99490, 99439, 99487, 99489)\n- Audit-ready documentation\n\n**Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM):**\n- Wearable sensor and home health monitor integration\n- Biometric data collection\n- Behavioral health–specific monitoring (mood, anxiety, sleep patterns)\n\n**Public Health Reporting:**\n- Immunization registry submission (certified (f)(1))\n- Syndromic surveillance (certified (f)(2))\n- Cancer case reporting (certified (f)(4))\n- Electronic case reporting (certified (f)(5))\n- Health care surveys (certified (f)(7))\n\n**Interoperability & Data Exchange:**\n- FHIR API access (certified (g)(7)–(g)(10))\n- C-CDA document exchange for transitions of care\n- Health Information Exchange (HIE) connectivity\n- Direct messaging\n- Integration with health information networks, payers, imaging services, and registries\n\n**Compliance & Reporting:**\n- MIPS/MACRA quality measure reporting\n- Clinical quality measures (47 CQMs evaluated per disclosures page)\n- ONC 2015 Edition Cures Update certification\n- HIPAA compliance tools\n- 42 CFR Part 2 behavioral health privacy support\n\n**AI Features (recent AI-driven claims scrubbing\n\n**Mobile:**\n- Avalon mobile EHR app (iOS/Android)\n- Mobile access to clinical and administrative functions\n\n### Data & Content\n\nBased on the features described above, CureMD SMART Cloud stores and manages the following categories of data:\n\n**Clinical data:** Patient demographics, medical histories, problem/diagnosis lists, medication lists, allergy lists, vital signs, clinical notes/encounter documentation, assessment and plans, clinical summaries, immunization records, lab orders and results, imaging/radiology orders and reports, referral records, schedules, registration/check-in records, referral records, document images (scans, faxes, x-rays), inventory records, multi-location organizational data.\n\n**Financial/billing data:** Charges, claims (submitted and adjudicated), payment records, denial records, patient balances, co-pay records, credit card transactions, eligibility verification records, payer contracts, financial reports, data (MIPS/MACRA/CQMs), public health reports (immunization registries, syndromic surveillance, cancer reporting, electronic case reporting), audit logs.\n\n**Communication data:** Secure messages (provider-to-provider, provider-to-patient), Direct messages, fax records, automated reminders, AI chatbot interactions.\n\n**RPM/CCM data:** Remote monitoring device readings, time logs, care portal), HAPI FHIR, Keycloak (authentication). Some certified features may require additional fees per the cost disclosure.\n\n---\n\n## Research Gaps\n\n- **Pricing structure:** CureMD does not publicly list pricing; the mandatory disclosures page mentions a separate cost disclosure document. It's unclear which features are included in the base product vs. add-ons.\n- **White-label/resale:** No evidence found that CureMD is a white-label or resold product. It appears to be a proprietary platform.\n- **On-premise option:** All evidence points to cloud-only deployment (\"SMART Cloud\"), though the company page does not explicitly address on-premise options.\n- **Acquisition history:** No evidence of recent acquisitions, mergers, or rebranding. The company appears to have operated continuously under the CureMD name since 1997.\n- **Detailed user reviews:** Software Advice and Capterra returned 403 errors; information from review sites was gathered via search result summaries rather than detailed review content. Reviews on PeerSpot give CureMD 9.0/10 overall. Common complaints include system bugs/slowness, billing module needing updates, and hidden fees.\n","numLines":187,"startLine":1,"totalLines":187}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-4-6","id":"msg_015UdFByaFe2gYrSAQ2rFDtj","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_017zVJaeqXmDkt9uNXZHoWPG","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/home/jmandel/hobby/ehi-export-analysis/results/curemd-com-inc/downloads/enrichment/extract-drs.ts","content":"#!/usr/bin/env bun\n/**\n * Extracts CureMD EHI Export DRS (Designated Record Set) data dictionary\n * from the XLSX file into queryable JSON.\n *\n * Input:  ../EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\n * Output: drs-data-dictionary.json, drs-summary.json, extraction-log.json\n */\n\nimport * as XLSX from \"xlsx\";\nimport { writeFileSync } from \"fs\";\nimport { join, dirname } from \"path\";\n\nconst scriptDir = dirname(new URL(import.meta.url).pathname);\nconst inputPath = join(scriptDir, \"..\", \"EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\");\nconst outputDir = scriptDir;\n\nconst wb = XLSX.readFile(inputPath);\n\n// --- Extract \"EHI Export\" overview sheet ---\nconst overviewSheet = wb.Sheets[\"EHI Export\"];\nconst overviewData = XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json(overviewSheet, { header: 1 }) as any[][];\nconst overviewText = overviewData\n  .map((row) => row.filter((c) => c != null).join(\" \"))\n  .filter((line) => line.trim().length > 0)\n  .join(\"\\n\");\n\n// --- Extract \"DRS\" data dictionary sheet ---\nconst drsSheet = wb.Sheets[\"DRS\"];\nconst drsRaw = XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json(drsSheet, { header: 1 }) as any[][];\n\ninterface Field {\n  name: string;\n  dataType: string;\n  description: string;\n}\n\ninterface DataClass {\n  name: string;\n  fields: Field[];\n}\n\nconst dataClasses: DataClass[] = [];\nlet currentClass: DataClass | null = null;\n\n// Row 0 is headers: Data Class | Data Elements | Data Type | Description\nfor (let i = 1; i < drsRaw.length; i++) {\n  const row = drsRaw[i];\n  const classCell = row[0] != null ? String(row[0]).trim() : \"\";\n  const fieldName = row[1] != null ? String(row[1]).trim() : \"\";\n  const dataType = row[2] != null ? String(row[2]).trim() : \"\";\n  const description = row[3] != null ? String(row[3]).trim() : \"\";\n\n  if (classCell) {\n    currentClass = { name: classCell, fields: [] };\n    dataClasses.push(currentClass);\n  }\n\n  if (currentClass && fieldName) {\n    currentClass.fields.push({ name: fieldName, dataType, description });\n  }\n}\n\n// --- Build outputs ---\nconst totalFields = dataClasses.reduce((sum, dc) => sum + dc.fields.length, 0);\n\nconst dataDictionary = {\n  source: \"CureMD EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\",\n  extractedAt: new Date().toISOString(),\n  sheets: wb.SheetNames,\n  overview: overviewText,\n  dataClasses,\n};\n\nconst summary = {\n  source: \"CureMD EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\",\n  extractedAt: new Date().toISOString(),\n  totalDataClasses: dataClasses.length,\n  totalFields,\n  dataClassSummary: dataClasses.map((dc) => ({\n    name: dc.name,\n    fieldCount: dc.fields.length,\n    fieldNames: dc.fields.map((f) => f.name),\n    dataTypes: [...new Set(dc.fields.map((f) => f.dataType))],\n  })),\n};\n\nconst log = {\n  extractedAt: new Date().toISOString(),\n  inputFile: \"EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\",\n  sheetsFound: wb.SheetNames,\n  totalRawRows: drsRaw.length,\n  totalDataClasses: dataClasses.length,\n  totalFields,\n  parseFailures: [] as string[],\n  notes: [\n    \"Row 0 is header row, skipped\",\n    \"Data class name is in column A, carried forward for rows where it is blank\",\n    \"Two sheets: 'EHI Export' (overview) and 'DRS' (data dictionary)\",\n  ],\n};\n\nwriteFileSync(\n  join(outputDir, \"drs-data-dictionary.json\"),\n  JSON.stringify(dataDictionary, null, 2)\n);\nwriteFileSync(join(outputDir, \"drs-summary.json\"), JSON.stringify(summary, null, 2));\nwriteFileSync(join(outputDir, \"extraction-log.json\"), JSON.stringify(log, null, 2));\n\nconsole.log(`Extracted ${dataClasses.length} data classes with ${totalFields} total fields`);\nconsole.log(`Output: drs-data-dictionary.json, drs-summary.json, extraction-log.json`);\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":1,"cache_creation_input_tokens":192,"cache_read_input_tokens":55583,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":192},"output_tokens":25,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"3d2cfbfd-6bb7-480c-9ddb-27663b6a2fca","uuid":"7d7ed937-23f4-45ac-8c6e-30ea15d6a10a"}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-4-6","id":"msg_01WdawYgPH4pcgnvzeqY4wcr","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"tool_use","id":"toolu_014qtPtveF6Vgw7kkj3kpTp5","name":"Write","input":{"file_path":"/home/jmandel/hobby/ehi-export-analysis/results/curemd-com-inc/ehi-export-report.md","content":"# CureMD.com, Inc. — EHI Export Documentation\n\nCollected: 2026-02-15\n\n## Source\n- Registered URL: https://www.curemd.com/ehi-export.asp\n- CHPL IDs: 11246\n- Product: CureMD SMART Cloud (version 10g, certified 2023-03-02)\n\n## Navigation Journal\n\n**Step 1: Initial probe**\n```bash\ncurl -sI -L \"https://www.curemd.com/ehi-export.asp\" -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0'\n```\nReturned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/html, 125,287 bytes. No redirects.\n\n**Step 2: Fetch and examine the page**\n```bash\ncurl -sL \"https://www.curemd.com/ehi-export.asp\" -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0' -o /tmp/curemd-ehi.html\n```\nThe page has a straightforward layout: a hero banner titled \"Electronic Health Information Export\", then a section titled \"170.315(b)(10) EHI Export\" with a brief explanation and a single download link to the DRS data dictionary.\n\n**Step 3: Search for documentation links**\n```bash\ngrep -oiE 'href=\"[^\"]*\\.(pdf|zip|xlsx|xls|csv|json|doc|docx|yaml|yml)[^\"]*\"' /tmp/curemd-ehi.html\n```\nFound two downloadable files:\n- `href=\"/PDF/CureMD.pdf\"` — linked from the site navigation (marketing brochure)\n- `href=\"EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\"` — the EHI export data dictionary (linked from the b(10) section)\n\n**Step 4: Download XLSX data dictionary**\n```bash\ncurl -sL \"https://www.curemd.com/EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\" -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0' -o downloads/EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx\n```\nVerified: `file` reports \"Microsoft Excel 2007+\", 101,490 bytes.\n\n**Step 5: Download CureMD PDF**\n```bash\ncurl -sL \"https://www.curemd.com/PDF/CureMD.pdf\" -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0' -o downloads/CureMD.pdf\n```\nVerified: `file` reports \"PDF document, version 1.6, 20 page(s)\", 1,280,945 bytes.\nContent: General marketing brochure covering EHR, billing, scheduling, specialties, etc. No EHI export–specific content. Included for completeness since it was on the page, but not an EHI export artifact.\n\n**Step 6: Screenshot**\nNavigated to the page in Chrome and captured a viewport screenshot. The page is a simple static HTML page — no SPA, no accordion, no login wall.\n\n**Step 7: Checked all links on the page**\nScanned all `href` attributes. No additional EHI-related links beyond the XLSX. Other links go to CureMD product pages, blog, login, privacy policy, etc. — none EHI-export related.\n\n## What Was Found\n\nCureMD's EHI export documentation consists of a single dedicated page and one XLSX file:\n\n### The Web Page (ehi-export.asp)\nThe page explicitly addresses 170.315(b)(10) with a brief but clear description:\n- EHI export is available for single-patient or population-level export\n- Single patient export can be initiated by system administrators without developer assistance\n- Population export requires a request, with updates delivered via email\n- Export format is **CSV files** for structured data, with documents and images exported in their **native formats**\n- All exports delivered as ZIP files\n\n### The Data Dictionary (EHI_Export_DRS.xlsx)\nThe XLSX has two sheets:\n\n**\"EHI Export\" sheet**: Repeats the overview from the web page, with an explicit reference to the public URL.\n\n**\"DRS\" (Designated Record Set) sheet**: A detailed data dictionary with **38 data classes** and **893 fields** (excluding empty trailing rows). Each field includes:\n- Data class name (e.g., \"Allergies\", \"Charges\", \"Patient Demographics\")\n- Field name (e.g., \"Allergy Name\", \"RxNorm\", \"Severity\")\n- Data type (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, float, bit, text, nvarchar, date)\n- Description (plain English explanation of each field)\n\nThe 38 data classes are:\n1. Allergies (15 fields)\n2. Appointments (20 fields)\n3. Cases (18 fields)\n4. Charges (82 fields)\n5. Chemo Admin (15 fields)\n6. Chemo Admin IVSites (6 fields)\n7. Chemo Plan (22 fields)\n8. Chemo Plan Diagnosis (7 fields)\n9. Chemo Plan Drugs (28 fields)\n10. Claims (16 fields)\n11. Complaints (6 fields)\n12. Diagnosis (18 fields)\n13. Disclosures (11 fields)\n14. Diseases History (21 fields)\n15. Documents & Images (exported in native formats, per the description)\n16. Electronic Remittance Advice (19 fields)\n17. Family History (12 fields)\n18. Hospitalization History (6 fields)\n19. Immunizations (20 fields)\n20. Medications (19 fields)\n21. Memos (8 fields)\n22. OBGYN History (52 fields)\n23. Orders (24 fields)\n24. Patient Consents (5 fields)\n25. Patient Contacts (20 fields)\n26. Patient Demographics (71 fields)\n27. Patient Education (6 fields)\n28. Patient Insurances (76 fields)\n29. Patient Note (16 fields)\n30. Payments (77 fields)\n31. Provider Notes (exported as HTML files)\n32. Referrals (23 fields)\n33. Results (29 fields)\n34. Risk (8 fields)\n35. Social History (65 fields)\n36. Surgery History (18 fields)\n37. Vitals A (23 fields)\n38. Vitals B (9 fields)\n\nTwo special classes — \"Documents & Images\" and \"Provider Notes\" — don't have tabular field definitions. Instead, the data dictionary notes that documents/images are exported in their native formats, and provider notes are exported as HTML files with a naming convention.\n\nThe SQL-style data types (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, etc.) indicate the CSV columns map closely to the underlying database schema. This is a genuine (b)(10) approach: exporting the database's designated record set as flat files rather than mapping to FHIR or another clinical standard.\n\n## Export Coverage Assessment\n\n### Data Domain Coverage\n\nCureMD's export documentation covers a genuinely broad range of data domains. This is one of the more thorough (b)(10) implementations — the data dictionary goes well beyond US Core/USCDI:\n\n**Well covered (with detailed field definitions):**\n- **Demographics** (71 fields) — comprehensive patient information\n- **Clinical data** — allergies, diagnoses, complaints, vital signs (split into Vitals A and Vitals B), immunizations, medications, results (labs), orders, disease history, family history, social history (65 fields — very detailed), surgery history, hospitalization history, OBGYN history (52 fields)\n- **Billing/financial** — charges (82 fields), claims (16 fields), payments (77 fields), electronic remittance advice (19 fields), patient insurances (76 fields). This is notable: many vendors omit billing data entirely from EHI exports.\n- **Specialty clinical data** — chemotherapy plans, chemo plan drugs, chemo plan diagnosis, chemo administration, chemo admin IV sites. This oncology-specific data is exactly the kind of specialty content that a proper (b)(10) export should include.\n- **Care coordination** — referrals (23 fields), patient education, patient consents\n- **Documents** — documents and images in native formats, provider notes as HTML\n- **Patient communications** — memos, patient notes\n- **Risk assessments** — risk data (8 fields)\n- **Cases** — case management data (18 fields)\n\n**Notably present (and often missing from other vendors):**\n- Billing records (charges, claims, payments, ERA) — often the biggest gap in EHI exports\n- Oncology/chemotherapy data — specialty-specific clinical data\n- OBGYN history — specialty-specific\n- Disclosures — information release tracking\n- Patient insurances — enrollment/coverage data\n- Appointments — scheduling data\n\n**Potentially missing or unclear:**\n- **Telehealth session records** — CureMD offers integrated telehealth, but no data class for video visit records appears in the export\n- **Chronic Care Management (CCM) data** — CureMD has a CCM module with care plans, time tracking, and engagement tracking, but no explicit CCM data class in the export. Care plan elements may be captured under other classes.\n- **Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) data** — CureMD integrates with wearables (Apple Watch, Fitbit), but device readings don't have their own data class\n- **Secure messages** — the patient portal supports secure messaging between patients and providers; no explicit \"Messages\" data class (though \"Memos\" and \"Patient Note\" may cover some of this)\n- **Care plans/goals** — no explicit care plan data class, though clinical notes and provider notes may embed this\n- **Growth charts / pediatric-specific data** — CureMD supports pediatrics but no pediatric-specific data class appears\n- **Behavioral health assessments** — CureMD supports behavioral health with screening tools (GAD-7, PHQ-9), but these may be captured under Results or Provider Notes rather than having dedicated fields\n\nThese gaps are relatively minor compared to many vendors. The missing domains are mostly specialty-module data that may be stored within the broader clinical note or results classes rather than as separate entities. The core clinical and financial data coverage is strong.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\n- **Format**: CSV files for structured data; native formats for documents and images; HTML for provider notes\n- **Delivery**: ZIP archive\n- **Standard**: Not FHIR, not C-CDA — this is a flat-file database export. The data types (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, float, bit, text, nvarchar) are SQL Server column types, indicating a direct mapping from the underlying relational database.\n- **Appropriateness**: For a (b)(10) export, CSV is a reasonable format. It's computable, universally readable, and can represent the full breadth of the database without the limitations of mapping to FHIR resource types. A third party could reconstruct the patient record from these CSVs, though understanding relationships between tables (e.g., linking charges to claims to ERA) would require understanding the shared key fields (Patient ID, Account Number, etc.).\n- **Relationship handling**: No explicit foreign key documentation or relationship diagram is provided. However, many tables share common fields (Practice, Patient ID, Account Number, Date/Time) that serve as implicit join keys. A developer would need to infer relationships from field names and descriptions.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\n- **Readability**: Good. The web page is clear and concise. The XLSX data dictionary is well-structured with consistent formatting.\n- **Data dictionary granularity**: Each field has a name, SQL data type, and plain English description. This is better than many vendors who only list table names or field names without descriptions.\n- **Value sets**: Not documented. Coded fields (e.g., \"Status\", \"Severity\", \"Type\") have descriptions but no enumeration of valid values. A developer importing this data would need to discover valid values from the data itself.\n- **Sample data**: None provided. No example CSV files or sample records.\n- **Worked examples**: None. No step-by-step walkthrough of performing an export or interpreting the output.\n- **Developer implementability**: A developer could understand the data model from this documentation, but importing the data would require some inference about relationships, coded values, and edge cases. The documentation is a solid data dictionary, but not a complete integration specification.\n- **Maintenance**: The XLSX is dated \"November 2023\" (per the \"Last Updated\" cell in the EHI Export sheet). The product was certified in March 2023, so this was updated ~8 months post-certification.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Field-level granularity**: Excellent — 893 fields across 38 data classes, each with data type and description\n- **Coded field value sets**: Not documented\n- **Relationships between entities**: Implicit (shared key fields) but not explicitly documented\n- **Versioning**: \"Last Updated: November 2023\" noted on the overview sheet\n- **Schema files**: None (no XSD, JSON Schema, DDL, or OpenAPI)\n\n### (b)(10) vs (g)(10) Assessment\n\nThis is a **genuine (b)(10) implementation**, not a repackaged (g)(10) FHIR API. Key evidence:\n1. The export format is CSV, not FHIR\n2. The data dictionary includes billing data (charges, claims, payments, ERA) which is not part of US Core\n3. Specialty clinical data (oncology/chemo) is included\n4. The data dictionary maps closely to the underlying relational database, not to FHIR resource types\n5. There is no mention of FHIR, Bulk Data, or US Core in the EHI export documentation\n6. Insurance/enrollment data is included with 76 fields — well beyond USCDI scope\n\nCureMD has done the work of defining their designated record set and documenting the database fields that make up the export. This is exactly what a (b)(10) implementation should look like.\n\n## Access Summary\n- Final URL (after redirects): https://www.curemd.com/ehi-export.asp\n- Status: found\n- Required browser: no (all content accessible via curl)\n- Navigation complexity: direct_link (XLSX linked directly from the page)\n- Anti-bot issues: none\n\n## Obstacles & Dead Ends\nNone. The page loaded cleanly, the XLSX downloaded without issues, and no authentication was required. The documentation was straightforward to locate and download. The CureMD.pdf found on the page is a marketing brochure unrelated to EHI export — included for completeness but not an EHI artifact.\n"},"caller":{"type":"direct"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":1,"cache_creation_input_tokens":390,"cache_read_input_tokens":61533,"cache_creation":{"ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,"ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":390},"output_tokens":25,"service_tier":"standard","inference_geo":"not_available"},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"3d2cfbfd-6bb7-480c-9ddb-27663b6a2fca","uuid":"237a7210-93d8-4220-984f-4a83aaeee6f3"}

Each field includes:\n- Data class name (e.g., \"Allergies\", \"Charges\", \"Patient Demographics\")\n- Field name (e.g., \"Allergy Name\", \"RxNorm\", \"Severity\")\n- Data type (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, float, bit, text, nvarchar, date)\n- Description (plain English explanation of each field)\n\nThe 38 data classes are:\n1. Allergies (15 fields)\n2. Appointments (20 fields)\n3. Cases (18 fields)\n4. Charges (82 fields)\n5. Chemo Admin (15 fields)\n6. Chemo Admin IVSites (6 fields)\n7. Chemo Plan (22 fields)\n8. Chemo Plan Diagnosis (7 fields)\n9. Chemo Plan Drugs (28 fields)\n10. Claims (16 fields)\n11. Complaints (6 fields)\n12. Diagnosis (18 fields)\n13. Disclosures (11 fields)\n14. Diseases History (21 fields)\n15. Documents & Images (exported in native formats, per the description)\n16. Electronic Remittance Advice (19 fields)\n17. Family History (12 fields)\n18. Hospitalization History (6 fields)\n19. Immunizations (20 fields)\n20. Medications (19 fields)\n21. Memos (8 fields)\n22. OBGYN History (52 fields)\n23. Orders (24 fields)\n24. Patient Consents (5 fields)\n25. Patient Contacts (20 fields)\n26. Patient Demographics (71 fields)\n27. Patient Education (6 fields)\n28. Patient Insurances (76 fields)\n29. Patient Note (16 fields)\n30. Payments (77 fields)\n31. Provider Notes (exported as HTML files)\n32. Referrals (23 fields)\n33. Results (29 fields)\n34. Risk (8 fields)\n35. Social History (65 fields)\n36. Surgery History (18 fields)\n37. Vitals A (23 fields)\n38. Vitals B (9 fields)\n\nTwo special classes — \"Documents & Images\" and \"Provider Notes\" — don't have tabular field definitions. Instead, the data dictionary notes that documents/images are exported in their native formats, and provider notes are exported as HTML files with a naming convention.\n\nThe SQL-style data types (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, etc.) indicate the CSV columns map closely to the underlying database schema. This is a genuine (b)(10) approach: exporting the database's designated record set as flat files rather than mapping to FHIR or another clinical standard.\n\n## Export Coverage Assessment\n\n### Data Domain Coverage\n\nCureMD's export documentation covers a genuinely broad range of data domains. This is one of the more thorough (b)(10) implementations — the data dictionary goes well beyond US Core/USCDI:\n\n**Well covered (with detailed field definitions):**\n- **Demographics** (71 fields) — comprehensive patient information\n- **Clinical data** — allergies, diagnoses, complaints, vital signs (split into Vitals A and Vitals B), immunizations, medications, results (labs), orders, disease history, family history, social history (65 fields — very detailed), surgery history, hospitalization history, OBGYN history (52 fields)\n- **Billing/financial** — charges (82 fields), claims (16 fields), payments (77 fields), electronic remittance advice (19 fields), patient insurances (76 fields). This is notable: many vendors omit billing data entirely from EHI exports.\n- **Specialty clinical data** — chemotherapy plans, chemo plan drugs, chemo plan diagnosis, chemo administration, chemo admin IV sites. This oncology-specific data is exactly the kind of specialty content that a proper (b)(10) export should include.\n- **Care coordination** — referrals (23 fields), patient education, patient consents\n- **Documents** — documents and images in native formats, provider notes as HTML\n- **Patient communications** — memos, patient notes\n- **Risk assessments** — risk data (8 fields)\n- **Cases** — case management data (18 fields)\n\n**Notably present (and often missing from other vendors):**\n- Billing records (charges, claims, payments, ERA) — often the biggest gap in EHI exports\n- Oncology/chemotherapy data — specialty-specific clinical data\n- OBGYN history — specialty-specific\n- Disclosures — information release tracking\n- Patient insurances — enrollment/coverage data\n- Appointments — scheduling data\n\n**Potentially missing or unclear:**\n- **Telehealth session records** — CureMD offers integrated telehealth, but no data class for video visit records appears in the export\n- **Chronic Care Management (CCM) data** — CureMD has a CCM module with care plans, time tracking, and engagement tracking, but no explicit CCM data class in the export. Care plan elements may be captured under other classes.\n- **Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) data** — CureMD integrates with wearables (Apple Watch, Fitbit), but device readings don't have their own data class\n- **Secure messages** — the patient portal supports secure messaging between patients and providers; no explicit \"Messages\" data class (though \"Memos\" and \"Patient Note\" may cover some of this)\n- **Care plans/goals** — no explicit care plan data class, though clinical notes and provider notes may embed this\n- **Growth charts / pediatric-specific data** — CureMD supports pediatrics but no pediatric-specific data class appears\n- **Behavioral health assessments** — CureMD supports behavioral health with screening tools (GAD-7, PHQ-9), but these may be captured under Results or Provider Notes rather than having dedicated fields\n\nThese gaps are relatively minor compared to many vendors. The missing domains are mostly specialty-module data that may be stored within the broader clinical note or results classes rather than as separate entities. The core clinical and financial data coverage is strong.\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\n- **Format**: CSV files for structured data; native formats for documents and images; HTML for provider notes\n- **Delivery**: ZIP archive\n- **Standard**: Not FHIR, not C-CDA — this is a flat-file database export. The data types (varchar, int, datetime, numeric, float, bit, text, nvarchar) are SQL Server column types, indicating a direct mapping from the underlying relational database.\n- **Appropriateness**: For a (b)(10) export, CSV is a reasonable format. It's computable, universally readable, and can represent the full breadth of the database without the limitations of mapping to FHIR resource types. A third party could reconstruct the patient record from these CSVs, though understanding relationships between tables (e.g., linking charges to claims to ERA) would require understanding the shared key fields (Patient ID, Account Number, etc.).\n- **Relationship handling**: No explicit foreign key documentation or relationship diagram is provided. However, many tables share common fields (Practice, Patient ID, Account Number, Date/Time) that serve as implicit join keys. A developer would need to infer relationships from field names and descriptions.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\n- **Readability**: Good. The web page is clear and concise. The XLSX data dictionary is well-structured with consistent formatting.\n- **Data dictionary granularity**: Each field has a name, SQL data type, and plain English description. This is better than many vendors who only list table names or field names without descriptions.\n- **Value sets**: Not documented. Coded fields (e.g., \"Status\", \"Severity\", \"Type\") have descriptions but no enumeration of valid values. A developer importing this data would need to discover valid values from the data itself.\n- **Sample data**: None provided. No example CSV files or sample records.\n- **Worked examples**: None. No step-by-step walkthrough of performing an export or interpreting the output.\n- **Developer implementability**: A developer could understand the data model from this documentation, but importing the data would require some inference about relationships, coded values, and edge cases. The documentation is a solid data dictionary, but not a complete integration specification.\n- **Maintenance**: The XLSX is dated \"November 2023\" (per the \"Last Updated\" cell in the EHI Export sheet). The product was certified in March 2023, so this was updated ~8 months post-certification.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\n- **Field-level granularity**: Excellent — 893 fields across 38 data classes, each with data type and description\n- **Coded field value sets**: Not documented\n- **Relationships between entities**: Implicit (shared key fields) but not explicitly documented\n- **Versioning**: \"Last Updated: November 2023\" noted on the overview sheet\n- **Schema files**: None (no XSD, JSON Schema, DDL, or OpenAPI)\n\n### (b)(10) vs (g)(10) Assessment\n\nThis is a **genuine (b)(10) implementation**, not a repackaged (g)(10) FHIR API. Key evidence:\n1. The export format is CSV, not FHIR\n2. The data dictionary includes billing data (charges, claims, payments, ERA) which is not part of US Core\n3. Specialty clinical data (oncology/chemo) is included\n4. The data dictionary maps closely to the underlying relational database, not to FHIR resource types\n5. There is no mention of FHIR, Bulk Data, or US Core in the EHI export documentation\n6. Insurance/enrollment data is included with 76 fields — well beyond USCDI scope\n\nCureMD has done the work of defining their designated record set and documenting the database fields that make up the export. This is exactly what a (b)(10) implementation should look like.\n\n## Access Summary\n- Final URL (after redirects): https://www.curemd.com/ehi-export.asp\n- Status: found\n- Required browser: no (all content accessible via curl)\n- Navigation complexity: direct_link (XLSX linked directly from the page)\n- Anti-bot issues: none\n\n## Obstacles & Dead Ends\nNone. The page loaded cleanly, the XLSX downloaded without issues, and no authentication was required. The documentation was straightforward to locate and download. The CureMD.pdf found on the page is a marketing brochure unrelated to EHI export — included for completeness but not an EHI artifact.\n","structuredPatch":[],"originalFile":null}}
